readme: THE GLOBAL FORBIDDEN PROSE LIST. Terms no recipe title and no reader-facing prose may carry, on any recipe, ever. It is the GLOBAL half of the per-spec forbidden_prose_terms field: that field is a per-recipe convention a writer opts into, this file is a rule every recipe is held to. One data file on purpose, so the PowerShell readers and any future Python reader read the same bytes and cannot drift apart.
ruling: Brad, 2026-09-12, backlog I138. 'A title we publish on a paid page is our claim, whatever blog it came from. No recipe title or reader-facing prose may carry a health word (healthy, clean, guilt-free, light, nutritious and the like) unless we own a written bar behind it. Source attribution lines naming the originating blog stay as they are. Add healthy to the global forbidden prose list so the Recipe Hunter cannot import the word again.'
enforced_by: meal-prep\pipeline\forbidden-prose-lib.ps1  - the one matcher and the one reader-facing field set
meal-prep\pipeline\build-v2-spec.ps1        - REFUSES to write a new spec carrying one (the Recipe Hunter's import door)
meal-prep\pipeline\spec-guards.ps1          - fails validation for an existing spec carrying one

meal-prep\pipeline\audit-forbidden-prose.ps1 - push-time gate over the whole committed catalogue, at zero. It lives here rather than in ops\ because its population is meal-prep\db\recipes, and an ops\ detector reading that is the coupling ops\audit-cross-module-reach.ps1 ratchets
attribution_is_exempt: credit_html, source_url and source_site are NOT swept. Brad's ruling says the source attribution line naming the originating blog stays as it is: 'Recipe adapted from The Clean Eating Couple' is a fact about where the recipe came from, not a claim we are making about the food. 16 of 584 recipes carry the word 'healthy' in an attribution field and every one of them is correct. The slug is exempt for a different reason: it is the live URL of a paid page, and changing it breaks every link and search result pointing at it.
a_brand_name_is_the_one_hard_case: If a PRODUCT we buy is literally branded with a listed word (Campbell's Healthy Request, say), it would land in ingredients_display and this gate would fire on a name we did not write. That has not happened: 0 of 584 recipes carry a listed term in ingredients_display today. When it does, it wants a ruling and a named exception on the row, not a quiet widening of the matcher.
matching: Case-insensitive, on WORD BOUNDARIES. A term with a hyphen matches its spaced form too (guilt-free finds 'guilt free'). Substring matching was rejected: it makes 'healthy' fire inside 'healthyfoodiegirl.com'.

terms.reason: Brad's ruling, I138, named explicitly. Was in two live paid titles, one of which is 5.5% vegetable by weight.
The same claim in another spelling. 0 of 584 today; listed so it cannot arrive as the workaround.

not_listed.reason: Brad's ruling names it, and a bare word-boundary ban on it is not implementable: measured 2026-09-12 over the reader-facing fields of all 584 recipes, 58 carry it and the uses are 'scrape the bottom of the pot clean' and 'rinse them clean'. Banning it would put the gate red on day one over 58 sentences that make no claim about health. The health-claim FORMS of it are listed above ('clean eating', 'eat clean'); the verb is not.

Same measurement: 67 of 584, and the uses are the product name 'Light Sour Cream (generic)', 'store it away from light', and 'light brown sugar'. A ban would fire on an ingredient's actual name. If we ever mean 'light' as a calorie claim it will be in a sentence, and the sentence will say so in words this list already holds.

NOT a health word, so it is not banned outright here. It is an FDA nutrient content claim, and since Brad's I143 ruling of 2026-09-19 it lives in nutrient_claims below: legal on a NEW recipe that clears its numeric bar, refused on one that does not.
A diet word rather than a health word. Not in Brad's I138 class. One live title carries it (Keto Turkey Broccoli Cheddar Casserole) and it is left standing on purpose.

nutrient_claims.readme: THE FDA NUTRIENT CONTENT CLAIM WORDS. Unlike the health words above, every one of these HAS a regulatory definition with a numeric condition, so it is not banned outright: a NEW recipe may use the word only where its own per-serving macros clear that condition, and a word whose condition needs a number the spec does not carry (sodium, sugars, fibre, saturated fat, cholesterol, or a reference food) cannot be shown to clear it and is refused. Read through meal-prep\pipeline\nutrient-claim-lib.ps1; measured over the live catalogue by meal-prep\pipeline\audit-nutrient-claims.ps1.
nutrient_claims.ruling: Brad, 2026-09-19, backlog I143: 'rule for new, measure old'. A NEW recipe may use an FDA-defined nutrient-content claim word only where the recipe meets that claim's FDA numeric bar computed from its own per-serving macros, enforced at publish time where the estate checks new recipes. The live catalogue is MEASURED, not swept: no live page changes on this ruling.
nutrient_claims.applies_to: NEW recipes only. Enforced at build-v2-spec's Write-Spec when the spec did not exist before the run (the Recipe Hunter's import door), and by wave-preaudit's nutrient-claims check on every wave slug. A rebuild of an existing spec is WARNED, never refused, because the old uses await Brad's ruling on a sweep.
sources: 21 CFR 101.13(m) - a main dish product weighs at least 6 oz per labeled serving (and meets food-group conditions not checked here)
21 CFR 101.9(c)(7)(iii) - the protein DRV is 50 g; 101.9(c)(7)(i) - a protein claim requires the PDCAAS-corrected amount
21 CFR 101.9(c)(9) - the dietary fibre Daily Value is 28 g
21 CFR 101.54(b) - high / rich in / excellent source of: 20 percent or more of the DV per RACC; 101.54(c) - good source / contains / provides: 10 to 19 percent; 101.54(d) - fibre claims

21 CFR 101.56(d)(1) - light / lite on a meal or main dish: meets the low calorie or the low fat definition; 101.56(e)(1) - light describing a physical or organoleptic attribute such as texture or colour is not a nutrient claim; 101.56(f) - nor is light that is part of a statement of identity (light brown sugar)

21 CFR 101.60(b)(1) - calorie free: less than 5 calories per RACC and per labeled serving; 101.60(b) - low calorie: 40 calories or less per RACC, and for a meal or main dish 120 calories or less per 100 g; 101.60(c)(1) - sugar free: less than 0.5 g sugars; 101.60(c)(2) - no added sugar
21 CFR 101.61(b) - sodium free under 5 mg; very low sodium 35 mg or less (main dish: per 100 g); low sodium 140 mg or less (main dish: per 100 g)

21 CFR 101.62(b)(1) - fat free: less than 0.5 g fat per RACC and per labeled serving; 101.62(b)(2) - low fat: 3 g or less per RACC; 101.62(b)(3) - low fat, meal or main dish: 3 g or less per 100 g and not more than 30 percent of calories from fat; 101.62(c) - saturated fat; 101.62(d) - cholesterol; 101.62(e)(3) and (e)(5) - lean and extra lean, meal or main dish: under 10 g (5 g) fat, 4.5 g (under 2 g) saturated fat and under 95 mg cholesterol per 100 g and per labeled serving
Read on law.cornell.edu (the LII copy of the eCFR) on 2026-09-19; ecfr.gov itself refused the fetch.
nutrient_claims.serving_basis: Per serving is the spec's own stat block (cal, protein, fat), which is what the card prints. Per 100 g divides by the serving weight, taken as the sum of ingredients_grams over servings: RAW weight, because the spec carries no cooked weight. That is a stated approximation in both directions (meat loses water, rice and pasta gain it). A serving of 170.1 g (6 oz) or more is judged by the main dish conditions; a lighter one by the per-RACC conditions with the serving standing in for the RACC.
nutrient_claims.not_applied: Two stricter readings are recorded and NOT applied, because the ruling names per-serving macros: 101.9(c)(7)(i) wants the PDCAAS-corrected protein for any protein claim (stat.protein is uncorrected, which overstates it most for plant proteins), and 101.54(b) lets a main dish carry 'high' only for an identified component food that is itself high in a RACC.
nutrient_claims.bar_kinds: Closed vocabulary; the lib throws on anything else. min_protein_g (value), lt_fat_g_per_serving (value), lt_cal_per_serving (value), low_fat, low_calorie, light, not_computable (missing).
nutrient_claims.product_variant_rule: A claim marked product_variant: true is also how a STORE names a product variant (fat free cottage cheese, 1/3 less fat cream cheese, low sodium broth, sugar-free BBQ sauce, a high fiber tortilla). An occurrence of one directly before a product word - a word of any ingredient this recipe buys, or one of product_nouns (the low-fat kind, the fat free version) - describes that product, not the dish, and is not counted. Claims NOT marked (high protein, low calorie, the light shapes) are dish words in practice: high-protein chicken bowls is a claim about the bowls, whatever chicken is.
nutrient_claims.exempt: An occurrence is NOT our claim, and is not counted, when (1) it sits in a field rendered from the ingredient list (ingredients_display, ingredients_grams, scaler, cost_lines, recipeIngredient), or (2) it sits immediately beside a word of an ingredient this recipe buys whose own name or buy label carries the same claim word (Fat Free Cheddar, BBQ Sauce (Sugar Free)), or (3) the claim is product_variant and it sits directly before a product word (see product_variant_rule), or (4) it matches that claim's exempt_contexts.

claims.label: light / lite (as a calorie or fat claim)
patterns: keep(?:s|ing)? (?:it|this|this one|this bowl|this dish|this recipe|the bowl|the dish) (?:light|lite)
claims.reason: Main dish: meets the low calorie or the low fat definition. The pattern is deliberately NARROW: light describing texture or colour (light and fluffy) is exempt by 101.56(e)(1), light brown sugar by 101.56(f), and light naming a product (light sour cream) or an unrelated sense (away from light, green light) is not a claim, so only the calorie-and-fat shapes are listed. Unsound by construction: a claim phrased some other way is not seen.

not_listed.reason: Banned OUTRIGHT by the terms list above (I138). Its FDA definition at 21 CFR 101.65 needs food-group equivalents and added-sugar, sodium and saturated-fat limits, none of which this estate records.
Not the defined term, and every live use is comparative (a lighter build, mash lighter). Listed nowhere; a calorie claim in that shape would want a reference food.
101.61(c) conditions, but in practice these name a product we buy (unsalted butter), which the ingredient carve-out already covers where the product's name carries it.
Not an FDA-defined term, which is exactly why it cannot clear a bar. Out of this ruling's scope (defined words only); recorded so its absence is a decision.
